title: Redvale Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Redvale wells have a median depth of 84 feet, but local records range to 620 feet. See yields, costs, risks and permit history.
h1: Redvale, Colorado Well Depths, Yields and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Redvale means understanding the well record before you rely on a listing description. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 230 permitted wells, including 140 recorded as constructed. Reported depths vary widely, while most reported wells produce a useful household supply.

The records point to a mixed sedimentary and alluvial setting, with many permits naming an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Use these figures to set expectations for a drilling bid, water testing, storage and the site work needed to build. Nearby Norwood, Naturita and Nucla provide useful regional context, but a neighboring well is still the best comparison for a specific parcel.

sections.heading: Redvale well depths vary more than the median suggests
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Redvale is 84 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 240 feet, so a bid based only on the median could be misleading. The 90th-percentile depth is 401 feet, and the deepest record reaches 620 feet.

More than half of the depth records are under 100 feet, while 20% fall from 100 to 300 feet and 22% from 300 to 600 feet. That spread reflects changing sedimentary and alluvial conditions, along with fractured-bedrock wells. For a buyer, ask a driller to price the likely target depth and a deeper contingency separately. Nearby wells on the same formation and side of the valley are more useful than a countywide average.

sections.heading: Most Redvale wells report a workable household yield
sections.html:
Only 14 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are useful but not a guarantee for an untested parcel. Among those reports, the median is 8.8 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.2 to 10.0 gallons per minute.

Reported production is concentrated in the 5-to-15-gallon-per-minute range, accounting for 79% of the yield records. Another 14% produce 1 to 5 gallons per minute, while 7% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute. A household well does not need a high continuous flow if the well, pump and storage tank are properly sized, but a driller should test the actual hole before you count on irrigation or other heavy use. Exempt household-use wells also have legal limits on use, including the 35-gpm pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water is generally shallow in the Redvale records
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth from ground surface down to standing water when the well is not being pumped. The Redvale median is 20 feet, and the middle half is 17 to 32 feet. That is a shallow reported water level compared with the range of drilling depths.

These records do not provide a water-level-by-decade series, so they do not establish a falling or rising long-term water-table trend. A shallow static level also does not tell you how much water the formation can deliver during pumping. Ask for the well construction report, static level, pump test and any available seasonal measurements. On a sloping lot, surface elevation and local drainage can make neighboring static levels look different even when the wells draw from a related water-bearing zone.

sections.heading: Redvale permit activity spans several generations
sections.html:
Permit records show activity from the 1960s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2023. The busiest decades were the 1990s with 54 permits and the 2000s with 51. Records show 31 permits in the 2010s and 26 in the 2020s, along with earlier activity in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s.

The most frequently named drillers are Gordon Smith And Company, also recorded as Smith, Gordon R., with 31 wells; Mccracken Well Drilling Inc, also recorded as Mccracken, Alan E., with 24; and Rex Wyatt Drilling Co, also recorded as Wyatt, Michael R., with 13. These names describe the permit history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, references and the exact scope of a new proposal before hiring anyone.

sections.heading: A median-depth Redvale well starts around $10,200 finished
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground modeled near Redvale, the typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 84-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $4,200 to $6,300.

A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $10,200 to $18,300 at that median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing, unusual grouting or longer utility runs can change the proposal. Since the middle half of wells reaches 240 feet, ask for pricing that explains what happens if drilling continues beyond the initial target. Get the pump size, casing and grout, testing, electrical, trenching and abandonment terms in writing rather than comparing only a per-foot rate.

sections.heading: Check water quality, low yield and the building site
sections.html:
There are 14 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles of Redvale and 13 historic mine features. No EPA Superfund or cleanup sites are mapped in that area. Those facts do not prove a problem on a particular lot, but they justify a baseline water test and a review of nearby land uses, drainage and mine history.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk remains site-specific, especially where permits name fractured-bedrock aquifers. Review neighboring well depths, yields and construction reports before closing. Septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, access for a drill rig, and separation between the well and septic system can affect where a home fits. Confirm the permit, allowed use, water-rights requirements and any augmentation-plan issue with Colorado DWR before construction.

sections.heading: Use neighboring wells to plan a Redvale lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not the townwide median. Pull DWR records for nearby wells, compare their depth, aquifer description, static water level and reported yield, then have a licensed driller inspect access and propose a target zone. The records show 215 wells naming an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, 14 naming Dakota and 1 naming Hermosa. No wells in this dataset name a Denver Basin aquifer.

For a purchase, make water availability and quality testing part of due diligence. For a new build, coordinate the well location with the septic system, driveway, electrical route and house foundation before excavation starts. Keep a separate allowance for a deeper hole or difficult site conditions. If the property will use more than ordinary household needs, verify the permit and water-rights position instead of assuming a domestic permit covers irrigation, stock or other uses.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Redvale, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Redvale is 84 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 240 feet, but records range to 620 feet. About 56% are under 100 feet, while 22% are between 300 and 600 feet. Nearby wells on the same ground are the best guide for a new site.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Redvale?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate near Redvale is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 84-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $4,200 to $6,300. A finished system including pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $10,200 to $18,300. Deeper drilling, access problems and extra construction can raise the final price.

faq.q: How much water do Redvale wells produce?
faq.a: Only 14 wells report pump yields, so the sample is limited. Those records show a median yield of 8.8 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.2 to 10.0. Most reported wells, 79%, produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. A pump test on the actual well is more important than the local median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Redvale?
faq.a: The local records identify 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 13 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped. That does not determine a parcel's water quality. Test a private well before purchase and after construction, using tests appropriate for local land uses and any nearby mine or contamination concern.

faq.q: Are there dry wells or low-yield wells near Redvale?
faq.a: The reported yield records show no wells under 1 gallon per minute, but only 14 wells report a yield. That small sample cannot eliminate dry-hole or low-yield risk on a new parcel, particularly in fractured-bedrock ground. Review neighboring construction reports and have a licensed driller evaluate the site before relying on a water-use plan.
